title: Capstone kickoff: room booking
idea: The capstone is one Meeting Room Booking System you take from requirements to a tested, documented design you can present and defend.
points: Fix the scope first: must-have requirements now, stretch goals later.
Write the public API of `BookingService` before any logic.
Each page of this chapter adds one layer to the same classes.
Keep the class names stable so every later step builds on them.

items.label: Scope
items.text: Must-haves: search, book, cancel, no double booking, notify. Recurring bookings wait.

items.label: Model
items.text: Turn requirements into use cases and entities such as `Room`, `Booking` and `Employee`.

items.label: Diagram
items.text: Draw the class diagram and the interfaces, such as `ConflictPolicy` and the repositories.

items.label: Build
items.text: Write `BookingService` and in-memory repositories, then run every use case as a script.

items.label: Harden
items.text: Add typed errors, `AuditLogger`, metrics, patterns and tests.

items.label: Present
items.text: Document with UML, then explain each trade-off in a review.

code.title: Scope as data
code.caption: Requirements get ids so classes and tests can point back to them. Mark `R6` as must-have and run again.

code.title: API before logic
code.caption: The three public methods are the use cases. Every body throws until a later page fills it in.

pitfalls: Agree the scope before coding; adding features mid-design hides the core trade-offs.
Do not start with recurring bookings; finish the must-have use cases first.
Avoid renaming core classes later; diagrams, tests and code drift apart.

quiz.why: A class prototype always owns `constructor` as well as each declared method. Nothing calls `book()`, so no error is thrown.

takeaway: Fix the scope and the public API before writing any logic.

starters: How do I decide what is in scope for an LLD interview?
Why write the public API before the implementation?
Which requirements would you cut if time runs short?
